lead: A held sample can take any value, but a converter stores it in a fixed number of bits, so it must round the sample to one of a finite set of levels. That rounding is quantization. The quantization error eq = Q(x) − x, the rounded value minus the true sample, behaves like a small added noise. That noise model links the number of bits to accuracy: it predicts the hiss of digital audio, the resolution of a sensor and the dynamic range of a converter. Only a few syllabi list quantization in this subject; where it is listed, exams ask for the step size, one rounded sample and the SQNR.
prereq: You need: where the held samples come from (see practical sampling), and the average power of a sinusoid, A²/2 (see Classification: energy, power, periodic, even and odd signals).

blocks.text: A uniform quantizer with n bits has L = 2ⁿ output levels. If its L steps exactly tile the input range from xmin to xmax, each step has width

blocks.where: Here Δ is the step size, also called the resolution, in volts; L = 2ⁿ is the number of levels and n the word length in bits.

blocks.text: This is the mid-rise quantizer: its levels sit at the middle of each step, at xmin + (k + ½)Δ for k = 0, 1, …, L − 1. For a 0 V to 8 V, 3-bit quantizer, L = 8, Δ = 1 V and the levels are 0.5 V, 1.5 V, …, 7.5 V. A mid-tread quantizer instead has a level at zero (levels at kΔ), so a zero input gives an exact zero output; its staircase is shifted by half a step, and a bipolar mid-tread quantizer uses an odd number of levels.

While the input stays inside the range, rounding to the nearest level gives |e<sub>q</sub>| ≤ Δ/2. For a busy signal the error changes from sample to sample in an unpredictable way, so it is modelled as random noise spread uniformly between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2. Its mean is 0 and its power (variance) is

blocks.where: Here P<sub>q</sub> is the quantization noise power in V². It follows from the mean of e² over a uniform spread: (1/Δ) ∫ e² de from −Δ/2 to Δ/2 = Δ²/12.

blocks.text: A full-scale sinusoid has amplitude A = (x<sub>max</sub> − x<sub>min</sub>)/2 = LΔ/2 and power A²/2 = L²Δ²/8. Dividing by Δ²/12 gives SQNR = 1.5L² = 1.5 × 4ⁿ. In decibels:

blocks.where: This holds for a full-scale sinusoid and uniform error. For a sine of smaller amplitude A, subtract 20 log₁₀(A<sub>fs</sub>/A) dB, where A<sub>fs</sub> = (x<sub>max</sub> − x<sub>min</sub>)/2.

blocks.text: Each extra bit halves Δ and adds about 6 dB. Inputs outside the range overload the quantizer: the output clips and the error can exceed Δ/2, so the noise model fails. Companding (μ-law in North America and Japan, A-law in India and Europe) compresses large amplitudes before a uniform quantizer and expands them after, which gives small signals smaller steps in volts; the SQNR then stays nearly constant over a wide range of input levels.

examples.question: A 3-bit uniform mid-rise quantizer covers 0 V to 8 V. Find L, Δ, the maximum error, the output and the error for an input sample of 3.4 V, the noise power, and the SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid.
steps: Maximum error inside the range = Δ/2 = 0.5 V.
3.4 V lies in the step from 3 V to 4 V, whose level is 3.5 V. Its distance to 3.5 V is 0.1 V and to 2.5 V is 0.9 V, so Q(3.4) = 3.5 V and e<sub>q</sub> = 3.5 − 3.4 = +0.1 V.
Full-scale sine: A = 4 V, power A²/2 = 8 V². SQNR = 8/(1/12) = 96, and 10 log₁₀ 96 = 19.82 dB. Check with the formula: 6.02 × 3 + 1.76 = 19.82 dB.
examples.answer: L = 8, Δ = 1 V, maximum error 0.5 V, Q(3.4 V) = 3.5 V with e<sub>q</sub> = +0.1 V, P<sub>q</sub> = 0.0833 V², SQNR = 19.82 dB.

traps: Using Δ as the maximum error. Inside the range the bound is Δ/2.
Writing L = 2ⁿ − 1. That is the largest code value; the number of levels is 2ⁿ.
Using 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a small or non-sinusoidal signal. It is for a full-scale sine with uniform error.
Mixing up the sign of the error: this book uses e<sub>q</sub> = Q(x) − x, so rounding 3.4 V up to 3.5 V gives +0.1 V.
Ignoring overload: outside x<sub>min</sub> to x<sub>max</sub> the output clips and Δ²/12 no longer describes the error.

quiz.a: Quantization maps each sample to the nearest of L allowed levels. Resolution is the step size Δ = (x<sub>max</sub> − x<sub>min</sub>)/L.

quiz.q: Why is quantization error modelled as uniform random noise?
quiz.a: For a busy signal the error jumps around unpredictably and is spread evenly between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, so it behaves like noise with zero mean and power Δ²/12.

quiz.q: A 4-bit quantizer covers −2 V to 2 V. Find L, Δ and the maximum error.
quiz.a: L = 2⁴ = 16; Δ = 4/16 = 0.25 V; maximum error Δ/2 = 0.125 V.

quiz.q: Estimate the SQNR of an ideal 10-bit quantizer for a full-scale sinusoid.
The 3-bit, 0 V to 8 V mid-rise quantizer receives 5.2 V. Find the output and the error. Is there overload?
quiz.a: 5.2 V lies in the 5 V to 6 V step, level 5.5 V. e<sub>q</sub> = 5.5 − 5.2 = +0.3 V, within ±0.5 V. The input is inside the range, so there is no overload.

quiz.q: A sine of amplitude 1 V feeds the 3-bit, 0 V to 8 V quantizer (centred at 4 V). Find its SQNR.
quiz.a: A<sub>fs</sub> = 4 V, so subtract 20 log₁₀(4/1) = 12.04 dB: SQNR = 19.82 − 12.04 = 7.78 dB. Check: (1²/2)/(1/12) = 6, and 10 log₁₀ 6 = 7.78 dB.

beyond: Real converters add a little random dither so the error really is noise-like, shape the noise out of the signal band, and use sigma-delta modulation for audio. A converter's measured SQNR gives its effective number of bits, ENOB = (SQNR − 1.76)/6.02. Search next: dither, noise shaping, sigma-delta ADC, ENOB.

figure.caption: Left: the 3-bit, 0 V to 8 V mid-rise quantizer climbs in steps of Δ = 1 V to the levels 0.5, 1.5, …, 7.5 V; the input 3.4 V is rounded to 3.5 V. Right: the error e<sub>q</sub> = Q(x) − x saws between +0.5 V and −0.5 V on every step and is +0.1 V at 3.4 V.
